MarketingTip.brief: A marketing psychology tip: one named psychological principle, why it happens in the human mind, and how marketers should apply it.
MarketingTip.structure: Curiosity hook, then a relatable story, everyday observation or real study, then name the principle, explain WHY it happens in the mind, show how it appears in marketing with a concrete example, end with an actionable takeaway.

BrandBreakdown.brief: A real, well-known brand's marketing decision decoded through the psychology behind it.
BrandBreakdown.structure: Hook that names the brand move as a puzzle, then what the brand actually did (only well-documented, public facts), then the psychological principle that explains why it works, then why it works on customers' minds, then how a smaller business can borrow the idea, end with an actionable takeaway. If you are not sure a fact about the brand is true, leave it out.

CopyClinic.brief: A before-and-after rewrite of a bland piece of marketing copy (headline, CTA button, pricing line, email subject, landing page line) using one psychological principle.
CopyClinic.structure: Hook about a common copy mistake, then a slide starting 'Before:' with a realistic bland example, then why it falls flat psychologically, then name the principle that fixes it, then a slide starting 'After:' with the rewritten version, then why the new version works in the reader's mind, optionally a second quick before/after, end with a takeaway the reader can apply to their own copy today. The before/after examples are invented illustrations, so never present them as real results or statistics.

MythOrMagic.brief: A popular marketing belief tested against what psychology research actually shows.
MythOrMagic.structure: Hook that states the belief as a question, then a slide starting 'The belief:' explaining why marketers believe it, then what the research actually found (only real, well-known findings), then the nuance (when the belief holds and when it does not), then what it means for marketers. The takeaway field is the verdict: start it with Myth, Magic, or It depends, then one practical line.

PsychInTheWild.brief: An everyday moment the reader has lived through (streaming autoplay, supermarket layouts, surge pricing, sale countdowns) and the psychological principle quietly working on them.
PsychInTheWild.structure: Hook that puts the reader inside the everyday moment, then describe what they experience, then reveal what is happening in their mind and name the principle, then explain why it works, then show how the same idea can be used ethically in their own marketing, end with an actionable takeaway.

MarketersAssemble.brief: A mindset post for marketers about the craft of marketing itself (uncertainty, experimentation, understanding prospects, marketers vs the world), still grounded in psychology.
MarketersAssemble.structure: Bold provocative hook, then a short series of punchy one-idea slides that build an argument about the craft of marketing, grounded in how people think, ending with a rallying line for marketers in the takeaway.

AIPsych.brief: Where AI meets buyer psychology: why people trust or resist AI (algorithm aversion, automation bias, the uncanny valley), how AI personalization, chatbots and AI-written content land in the customer's mind, and how marketers can use AI without losing what makes people buy from people.
AIPsych.structure: Tension hook about AI in marketing, then the everyday AI moment the reader knows (a chatbot, an AI ad, a recommendation, an AI-written email), then name the psychological principle at work, then why the mind reacts that way, then how a marketer should use or avoid it, end with a practical takeaway. Only cite real, well-known research; describe tools generically (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and similar) and never invent product features or numbers.

Autopilot.brief: How marketing and business work is being automated: funnels, lead pipelines, workflows, AI agents and no-code automations across social media, content, websites, lead capture, email, CRM, ads, sales follow-up, support and reporting. Practical, current and useful to a small team or a solo marketer. Not about psychology.
Autopilot.structure: Hook naming a task or process people still do by hand (or a shift in how work gets done, such as AI agents), then what it costs done manually, then the automated version as a short chain (trigger, tool or agent, action, result), then setup tips and the one mistake to avoid, then where a human should stay in the loop, end with a takeaway the reader can set up this week. Cover the whole field: funnels, pipelines, workflows, integrations, AI agents and assistants, not just one company's setup. Name widely used tools generically (Zapier, Make, n8n, HubSpot, Google Sheets, ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, website forms, email platforms, CRMs, GitHub Actions) and never invent features, prices, statistics or results. Only describe something as our own setup when it is in the facts below; most posts should not mention our setup at all.
facts: This page's posts are written by AI, designed in code, turned into Reels, and posted automatically every day through GitHub Actions and the Instagram API.
A human (the founder) approves every carousel and Reel in a small phone app before it goes live.
The same app shows each post's views, reach, saves and shares, fetched automatically every two hours.

design.about: Each series gets its own look. style: poster, editorial, essay, notebook or classic (the old plain look). accent: the highlight colour.

format.about: How posts are written. style: bullets (the save-first format from 22 Oct 2026: tension hook, 2 or 3 short bullet lines per slide, a 'Save this' line on the last body slide, and a final slide asking people to comment the keyword) or classic (the older sentence slides). cta.keyword is the word people comment; cta.offer is what you send them by DM.

closing_slide.text: Follow **{handle}** to learn the psychology underneath marketing.

writing.spelling: American English (color, realize, behavior, specialized, program). The audience is mostly in the US.
writing.voice: We-voice of a consumer-psychology-driven marketing collective. Smart, plain, a little playful. Talks to marketers, designers, freelancers, founders and small business owners, mostly in the US.
extra_rules: Avoid negative parallelism such as 'it's not X, it's Y' or 'not just X but Y'.
Use the serial (Oxford) comma in lists of three or more.

telegram.about: only_live: true means Telegram only tells you when a post has gone live. Everything else (drafts to approve, reminders, problems) is in the app.

audience.about: Who the posts are for. Change these lines to switch audience (India until 22 Oct 2026, US from then).
audience.examples: Use examples that make sense to a US audience (US brands, apps and everyday life such as Amazon, Target, Starbucks, Netflix, Costco, Apple, Spotify, DoorDash, Black Friday, Super Bowl ads), while staying understandable worldwide.
audience.money: Write every price and money amount in US dollars with the $ sign (for example $29 or $1,200). Never use rupees, Rs or INR.

reels.about: Reels made from each carousel. make: build a Reel for every draft (shown in the app). post: off, both (carousel and Reel at the same time) or reel (the Reel instead of the carousel). share_to_feed: true shows the Reel in your profile grid and followers' feeds too; false keeps it in the Reels tab only.

stats.about: Views, reach, likes, comments, saves and shares for each live post, fetched from Instagram every 2 hours and shown in the app's History.

format_reels.about: Slot 2 Reels. formats: the formats picked at random (remove any you don't want). voice needs the voice package (installed by the workflows); stock needs a PIXABAY_API_KEY (or PEXELS_API_KEY) secret.
